content_html:
I’ve shared the stories behind the Fiddler Web Debugger a fair bit over the years, in the Fiddler Book, in a talk at the CodeMash conference in 2015, and on this blog. It features prominently in my to-be-completed (some day?) memoir, and I’ve enjoyed telling Fiddler stories to folks who ask over the years. (I’ve also written a ton of content about using Fiddler.)

Over two decades, what was once a little side project came to influence a very meaningful percentage of my life, including where I live today and so many of my life’s experiences.

On Monday morning, I got a ping from someone from Progress Software, acquirers of Telerik in 2014, after Telerik acquired Fiddler (and for a few years, me) back in 2012. They asked for an email address to which they could send a note.

“This isn’t gonna be good“, I assumed. Correctly.

After I left Telerik for Google in 2016, development on the “Fiddler Classic” application had stagnated as the owners put their investments into a series of products they could monetize.

To be fair, this pivot was not unexpected. Initially, Telerik had purchased Fiddler largely for the community attention: the tool had a huge userbase of the exact developers the company was courting. Still, we always expected that eventually we’d have a cross-platform version of the product (a highly-requested improvement), and that non-Windows version could be sold like Telerik’s other professional tools.

Fiddler: Free Forever?

Telerik had loudly promised that Fiddler would remain “free forever” to avoid expected community outrage about commercializing a previously-free tool. Before Telerik, I had spoken to one potential acquirer who estimated the brand damage of their commercializing another previously-free tool at 25x their acquisition price, meaning they’d likely never turn a profit on it.

Telerik’s blog post announcing the change was explicit:

… but even that wasn’t enough, so a follow-up post was made shortly after:

The unambiguous clarity of this promise had meant that improving the “Fiddler Business” meant we’d need to: 1) monetize the technology behind Fiddler (we had several solid ideas), or 2) pivot to a new cross-platform product they could sell, or 3) renege on their promise and start charging for Fiddler for Windows, or 4) use Fiddler to showcase (and juice sales of) Telerik’s .NET component products.

While I was at Telerik, I worked a little on #1 — we created a licensable version of FiddlerCore, the core engine inside Fiddler, with the idea that other companies could sell products based on it. Telerik had used FiddlerCore inside their Test Studio product (that’s how I came to their attention to start with), and we assumed that other companies might want similar technology. Interest was… not very high… in part because we made little effort to evangelize, and partly because the license price would limit it to larger companies.

Very frustratingly and humiliatingly, my former employer wanted to use FiddlerCore inside their Message Analyzer product. But they didn’t want to pay for it. So instead, the software juggernaut worth hundreds of billions of dollars wrote code to prompt the end-user to pirate FiddlerCore:

This is the sort of behavior then most often seen from shady apps trying to avoid paying MP3 patent fees. To this day, I remain shocked that the lawyers from both companies allowed this experience to ship. (The fact that Microsoft-ecosystem developers made up virtually all of Telerik’s customers probably had something to do with Telerik not suing).

Days after I started at Telerik, I started work on strategy #2 (build a cross-platform version). I spent months trying to get Fiddler running on Mono, an early cross-platform version of the .NET Framework that ran on Mac and Linux. It didn’t go great. I built a serviceable version for Linux, but the UI port for MacOS would crash constantly. A hybrid strategy, using Mono for FiddlerCore, and building a new front-end on Electron, seemed like a plausible path forward. Alas, this vision was put on pause in 2014 after Telerik conducted broad US-based layoffs in advance of an expected IPO on the US stock market. After its aborted IPO and subsequent acquisition by Progress Software, Telerik eventually restarted this strategy, eventually shipping Fiddler Everywhere. Fiddler Everywhere offered several key advantages over the Windows-only Fiddler Classic (cross platform! some team features!) but it also had many shortcomings (fewer features, no extensibility model).

I’d hoped that Progress/Telerik might open-source Fiddler Classic at some point in order to grow the ecosystem— things like the Fiddler SAZ format would get even more popular and create the possibility of monetizable synergies. Alas, this never happened. Instead, Fiddler Classic just quietly decayed. As browsers adopted new standards (e.g. http2, h3, GREASE, tls1.3, zstd content compression), Fiddler Classic required more and more caveats and workarounds for continued use. However, Fiddler’s rich extensibility model means that I could keep building new capabilities in and on Fiddler in the ten years since I lost the ability to commit updates to Fiddler’s source directly.

I still use Fiddler on Windows almost every single day, but in many cases I’m not even using Fiddler to capture traffic anymore, instead just using it as a viewer for traffic captured natively by Chromium, or to use its TextEncoder and Inspectors, or even as a frontend for other tools.

Progress added a pre-download survey to collect user emails (annoying!) and periodically added surveys and advertisements directly inside the Fiddler Classic UI. But even if those were sometimes gratingly misleading, they weren’t too annoying.

Other changes of dubious value were also only mildly annoying.

This Week’s Rug Pull

Opening Fiddler on Monday, I was presented with a Fiddler Update announcement, including some neat improvements, particularly support for ZSTD decompression (obsoleting my workaround):

However, I didn’t accept the update straight away because I suspected something was afoot. (I also got distracted because Windows complained about the installer’s signature).

Sure enough, the first screen of the installer mentions another IMPORTANT change in Fiddler that was not mentioned in that shiny update announcement:

Progress Telerik has decided to start demanding Fiddler Classic not be used for “commercial” purposes. Beyond the new text in the license, Fiddler shows this big orange bar:

So… it appears that the owners of Fiddler have reneged on their promise to the community and the product is no longer free.

Dialogue with Progress/Telerik

Taken literally, the license agreement says you cannot use Fiddler Classic for commercial purposes, even if you pay! This is rather shocking, because it means that Fiddler’s most engaged users, who’ve built extensions and workflows around Fiddler, cannot use them, even if they’re willing to pay up. Such a position seems so wildly foolish that I assumed it must just be an oversight. I inquired, and Progress Telerik provided the following statement:

No, Progress is not planning to offer Fiddler Classic under a paid licence. 

We recognise the important role Fiddler Classic has played in supporting developers’ debugging workflows over many years. Continuing to invest in the product at the level required for commercial and enterprise customers, including ongoing feature development and platform modernisation, is not aligned with our long-term product strategy.  Accordingly, in recent years, Progress has focused on maintaining and supporting Fiddler Classic, while directing its development efforts towards Fiddler Everywhere.  

That said, we recognise the value of the extensibility capabilities available in Fiddler Classic. As a result, we will continue to work on scripting functionality in Fiddler Everywhere to help users continue their existing workflows with minimal disruption. We will also continue to evaluate additional feature requests based on customer needs and use cases. As always, we remain open to feedback and are committed to understanding how we can best support our users. 

Improved scripting functionality may satisfy some users, but it definitely will not encompass the wide range of scenarios enjoyed by Fiddler Classic today, especially for users who’ve built custom Inspectors, Transcoders, or other extensions that integrate Fiddler with other systems and processes used within their companies.

In a closing paragraph of their response, the Progress/Telerik product manager (or, more likely, their lawyer) appears to have attempted to suggest that I shouldn’t share my thoughts with you fine folks (emphasis mine):

Last but not at least, no person outside Progress is authorized to make announcements, provide comments, or respond to customers’ inquiries regarding Progress’ business on behalf of the company. All questions should be directed to Progress’ official communication channels fiddler@progress.com. 

Needless to say, I don’t speak on behalf of my former employer, but they’re also not going to stop me from talking about this change.

My Feelings

Some folks have asked how I feel about this. In short, disappointed, somewhat betrayed, but ultimately not surprised. Fiddler for Windows is a powerful tool that provides a tremendous amount of value to its users, and the nature of short-term profit maximization is that companies with valuable assets often struggle to recognize the long-term value of not abusing their users.

As I talked about previously in my post about mistakes I made when building Fiddler, my lack of a monetization plan was a key shortcoming in the product’s strategy. When Telerik acquired Fiddler, I assumed that the business folks there would develop a strategy beyond “monetizing the eyeballs” of the tens of thousands of weekly downloaders (although it was a bargain for that traffic acquisition alone).

As I’ve described above, development of a monetizable product strategy never got any real attention. Meanwhile, the team over at Postman hypothesized that a team-based product would be a winner, they tailored their offering accordingly, and their valuation skyrocketed to $5.6B after $433M in VC funding. I suspect that Postman’s true pre-IPO valuation may be lower, but for perspective, Progress Software’s entire market capitalization is currently just $1.7B.

I was excited to recently see Progress move Fiddler Everywhere toward the hottest trend in tech (Artificial Intelligence) by introducing support for MCP and the popular agents. Done right, this could be a killer feature that people are willing to pay big money for because of the value it can deliver.

However, I worry that Progress may have just vaporized the trust and goodwill that would’ve smoothed their plan to move users from a solid (if outdated) free product to an actively-developed paid product with a disjoint feature set. That’s especially true because Fiddler’s Session Archive Zip (SAZ) format could’ve allowed compatibility between the two.

Where Do We Go From Here?

Many Fiddler Classic users can happily continue to use the product for free for their personal non-commercial needs. Some Fiddler Classic customers may be happy to switch to Fiddler Everywhere with prices starting at $84/user/year for a feature-limited version of the product, or $444/user/year for the full Fiddler Everywhere feature set (which does not, as noted above, have all of Fiddler Classic’s features or compatibility with its extensions).

Some users have told me that they’ve be taking measures to disable Fiddler 5.x’s upgrade logic and remain on the final free version forever under its original license. They’ll use the extensibility model to keep it compatible with the modern web. Unfortunately, public redistribution of the older installer is not permitted under its license.

Some users will likely just stop using Fiddler entirely. As browser developer tools have evolved, many web developers’ needs are now fully met by the Network tab in their respective browsers.

Some users will likely move to competitive products, whether pay (Postman, Charles) or free open-source (mitmproxy).

Fiddler -> CLeARINET?

One thing that’s particularly baffling about Progress’ decision is the timing. Crippling Fiddler might’ve made some (evil) sense back in 2020 or so, but if you haven’t noticed, times have changed.

  • AI agents have enabled vibe-coding of production-quality code rapidly and cheaply. When a pre-Telerik acquirer asked me how long it would take them to implement their own, I guessed about 2000 hours, or about 700 if I guided them. Using an AI coding agent, I suspect you could get 90% of the way there in about 160 hours.
  • Much of the work in building Fiddler was in “figuring stuff out”, and the resources for doing that are dramatically better than ever before: we have better blogs, better tooling, better RFCs, and more open-source code than ever before.
  • The .NET platform is dramatically more capable (particularly related to async) than the v2.0 framework that Fiddler mostly targeted. I’ve already laid out a set of mistakes and pitfalls to avoid.
  • There’s a large community of .NET developers who might be interested in lending a hand, including many hundreds that recently voluntarily retired from Microsoft. And there are some amazingly bright developers (Kevin, Jérôme, Chrisx3, etc) who have built extensions and other code for legacy Fiddler who might jump at the chance to get their PRs into an open-source replacement.
  • Fiddler has no “moat” — the SAZ file format is simple and easily read and written. The product is designed to interact with protocols and formats based on open-standards. The true value of Fiddler was almost entirely “goodwill.”

Times seem ripe for a change.

When I named Fiddler, I did so because I was on the Microsoft Office clipart team and I knew we had plenty of free pictures of violins handy. Time has passed, and we have AI that can generate any images we want. An important kid in my life plays clarinet. If you squint at it, Clarinet sounds kinda like “Clear INET”, and seeing internet traffic in the clear is the whole point here.

In about 5 minutes, we’ve got a name, a domain, and a splash screen.

Now we just need some code. :)

I’m currently in an especially busy period at work and in life (I’m moving houses this month) but I hope to have some progress and updates in this space sometime soon. Unless Progress Software wants to save me the trouble and win tons of kudos for open-sourcing FiddlerClassic themselves! ;-)

-Eric

Appendix: Fiddler Origins

This section is from the Fiddler Book.

First, a confession—the Fiddler Web Debugger is not the result of a grand vision or the ambition to develop the world’s most popular debugging proxy. A tool born of necessity, I never set out to build a platform so flexible, powerful, and complicated that I’d be forced to spend a year writing a book to explain how to fully take advantage of it. But here we are.

Before diving into the technical chapters, I will begin by sharing the story behind how Fiddler came to be.

As a student at the University of Maryland in the spring of 1999, I had the chance to interview for a Program Management internship on a new team at Microsoft. One of my final interviewer’s first questions was “How does HTTP work?” Knowing only the basics, I gave an incomplete and somewhat inaccurate answer, but didn’t embarrass myself too badly. That summer and the following, I worked on features for the first version of SharePoint. On rare occasions, I found myself looking at web traffic in Microsoft Network Monitor (NetMon), a powerful but then primitive and difficult-to-use packet sniffer. In the early summer of 2001, I joined Microsoft full-time as the Program Manager for the Office Clip Art client and website.

At that time, most of the developers and testers working on my team were new to web development, having previously been responsible for writing native code applications in C and C++. It was quickly apparent that the debugging process was overly cumbersome—many of my colleagues were loath to use NetMon. I even watched some developers debugging HTTP requests by hovering over variables in Visual Studio, examining the raw traffic in hex:

Having developed several small Windows utilities, I was confident that I could code something to make web debugging simpler. My first simplistic effort was based on taking an existing C++ proxy server and making minor modifications to it so that it would spew HTTP traffic to the system console:

It’s generous to call this effort primitive—the proxy couldn’t handle secure traffic or authentication protocols. Non-text content was another problem—comically, the utility would try to render binary content as ASCII. Old-school console users may recall that the octet 0x07 represents the “bell” character, and when it’s displayed in the console, a system beep is played. Soon after its release, the hallways of the Office Online team sounded like a Las Vegas casino, as binary content flowed through the debug proxies running in each tester’s office.

Despite the very annoying limitations, this tool was still popular, and I was inspired to get started on the next version. I mocked up a quick little demo in Borland Delphi, a native code language used for most of my development work at the time. The colorful UI foreshadowed Fiddler’s eventual appearance:

However, as I pondered the security and memory-management implications of writing a proxy server in native code, I soon decided that my next effort would be developed in C#, a new language being developed by the Visual Studio team that my best friend had just joined. The notion of writing a HTTP proxy server from scratch in .NET posed just two significant challenges: I didn’t really know how HTTP worked, and I didn’t know how to code in C#.

Fortunately, given a few trips to the bookstore and a lot of spare weekends, both shortcomings would be remedied. Two books were my constant companions: HTTP: The Definitive Guide and the C# Cookbook. Chapter by chapter, I learned about HTTP and C#, and week-by-week Fiddler came to life. About six months after I started, I had a basic version of Fiddler ready:

Like its predecessors, it too had a large number of limitations (and thousands of bugs) but it was eagerly adopted by colleagues whose PC speakers were in danger of burning out from the incessant beeps of my first proxy utility.

Over the subsequent years, Fiddler was progressively enhanced with two extensibility models, a mechanism to automatically generate and modify responses, and support for secure (HTTPS) traffic, FTP, and HTML5 WebSockets. In 2012, Fiddler was ported to the Mono Framework, enabling it to run directly on Mac and Linux PCs and virtual machines.

It was quickly apparent that the debugging process was overly cumbersome—many of my colleagues were loath to use NetMon. I even watched some developers debugging HTTP requests by hovering over variables in Visual Studio, examining the raw traffic in hex: Having developed several small Windows utilities, I was confident that I could code something to make web debugging simpler. My first simplistic effort was based on taking an existing C++ proxy server and making minor modifications to it so that it would spew HTTP traffic to the system console: It’s generous to call this effort primitive—the proxy couldn’t handle secure traffic or authentication protocols. Non-text content was another problem—comically, the utility would try to render binary content as ASCII. Old-school console users may recall that the octet 0x07 represents the “bell” character, and when it’s displayed in the console, a system beep is played. Soon after its release, the hallways of the Office Online team sounded like a Las Vegas casino, as binary content flowed through the debug proxies running in each tester’s office. Despite the very annoying limitations, this tool was still popular, and I was inspired to get started on the next version. I mocked up a quick little demo in Borland Delphi, a native code language used for most of my development work at the time. The colorful UI foreshadowed Fiddler’s eventual appearance: However, as I pondered the security and memory-management implications of writing a proxy server in native code, I soon decided that my next effort would be developed in C#, a new language being developed by the Visual Studio team that my best friend had just joined. The notion of writing a HTTP proxy server from scratch in .NET posed just two significant challenges: I didn’t really know how HTTP worked, and I didn’t know how to code in C#. Fortunately, given a few trips to the bookstore and a lot of spare weekends, both shortcomings would be remedied. Two books were my constant companions: HTTP: The Definitive Guide and the C# Cookbook. Chapter by chapter, I learned about HTTP and C#, and week-by-week Fiddler came to life. About six months after I started, I had a basic version of Fiddler ready: Like its predecessors, it too had a large number of limitations (and thousands of bugs) but it was eagerly adopted by colleagues whose PC speakers were in danger of burning out from the incessant beeps of my first proxy utility. Over the subsequent years, Fiddler was progressively enhanced with two extensibility models, a mechanism to automatically generate and modify responses, and support for secure (HTTPS) traffic, FTP, and HTML5 WebSockets. In 2012, Fiddler was ported to the Mono Framework, enabling it to run directly on Mac and Linux PCs and virtual machines. sentences.en: My Feelings

blocks.html_en: Some folks have asked how I feel about this. In short, disappointed, somewhat betrayed, but ultimately not surprised. Fiddler for Windows is a powerful tool that provides a tremendous amount of value to its users, and the nature of short-term profit maximization is that companies with valuable assets often struggle to recognize the long-term value of not abusing their users.

sentences.en: Some folks have asked how I feel about this.

sentences.en: In short, disappointed, somewhat betrayed, but ultimately not surprised.
sentences.zh: 简而言之，失望，有些背叛，但最终并不感到惊讶。

sentences.en: Fiddler for Windows is a powerful tool that provides a tremendous amount of value to its users, and the nature of short-term profit maximization is that companies with valuable assets often struggle to recognize the long-term value of not abusing their users.
sentences.zh: Fiddler for Windows 是一款功能强大的工具，可为用户提供巨大的价值，而短期利润最大化的本质是，拥有宝贵资产的公司往往很难认识到不滥用用户的长期价值。

blocks.html_en: As I talked about previously in my post about mistakes I made when building Fiddler, my lack of a monetization plan was a key shortcoming in the product’s strategy. When Telerik acquired Fiddler, I assumed that the business folks there would develop a strategy beyond “monetizing the eyeballs” of the tens of thousands of weekly downloaders (although it was a bargain for that traffic acquisition alone).

blocks.html_en: As I’ve described above, development of a monetizable product strategy never got any real attention. Meanwhile, the team over at Postman hypothesized that a team-based product would be a winner, they tailored their offering accordingly, and their valuation skyrocketed to $5.6B after $433M in VC funding. I suspect that Postman’s true pre-IPO valuation may be lower, but for perspective, Progress Software’s entire market capitalization is currently just $1.7B.

blocks.html_en: However, I worry that Progress may have just vaporized the trust and goodwill that would’ve smoothed their plan to move users from a solid (if outdated) free product to an actively-developed paid product with a disjoint feature set. blocks.html_en: One thing that’s particularly baffling about Progress’ decision is the timing. Crippling Fiddler might’ve made some (evil) sense back in 2020 or so, but if you haven’t noticed, times have changed.

blocks.html_en: • AI agents have enabled vibe-coding of production-quality code rapidly and cheaply. When a pre-Telerik acquirer asked me how long it would take them to implement their own, I guessed about 2000 hours, or about 700 if I guided them. Using an AI coding agent, I suspect you could get 90% of the way there in about 160 hours.

blocks.html_en: • Much of the work in building Fiddler was in “figuring stuff out”, and the resources for doing that are dramatically better than ever before: we have better blogs, better tooling, better RFCs, and more open-source code than ever before.

blocks.html_en: First, a confession—the Fiddler Web Debugger is not the result of a grand vision or the ambition to develop the world’s most popular debugging proxy. A tool born of necessity, I never set out to build a platform so flexible, powerful, and complicated that I’d be forced to spend a year writing a book to explain how to fully take advantage of it. blocks.html_en: As a student at the University of Maryland in the spring of 1999, I had the chance to interview for a Program Management internship on a new team at Microsoft. One of my final interviewer’s first questions was “How does HTTP work?” Knowing only the basics, I gave an incomplete and somewhat inaccurate answer, but didn’t embarrass myself too badly. That summer and the following, I worked on features for the first version of SharePoint. On rare occasions, I found myself looking at web traffic in Microsoft Network Monitor (NetMon), a powerful but then primitive and difficult-to-use packet sniffer. In the early summer of 2001, I joined Microsoft full-time as the Program Manager for the Office Clip Art client and website.

content_html_zh:
多年来，我在 Fiddler 书籍、2015 年 CodeMash 会议的演讲以及本博客中分享了很多 Fiddler Web 调试器背后的故事。 它在我即将完成的（有一天？） 回忆录，多年来我很喜欢向那些询问的人讲述 Fiddler 的故事。 （我还写了大量有关使用 Fiddler 的内容。）

二十多年来，曾经的一个小副业项目对我生活中非常有意义的部分产生了影响，包括我今天居住的地方以及我一生的许多经历。

周一早上，我收到了来自 Progress Software 的人的 ping，该公司是 Telerik 在 2014 年的收购者，2012 年 Telerik 收购了 Fiddler（几年来，我也收购了）。 他们要求提供一个可以发送便条的电子邮件地址。

“这不会是好事”，我想。 正确。

2016 年我离开 Telerik 加入 Google 后，“Fiddler Classic”应用程序的开发陷入停滞，因为所有者将投资投入到一系列可以货币化的产品中。

平心而论，这次转向并不出人意料。 最初，Telerik 购买 Fiddler 主要是为了引起社区的关注：该工具拥有庞大的用户群，正是该公司正在吸引的开发人员。 尽管如此，我们始终期望最终我们能够拥有该产品的跨平台版本（这是一项强烈要求的改进），并且非 Windows 版本可以像 Telerik 的其他专业工具一样出售。

Fiddler：永远免费？

Telerik 曾大声承诺 Fiddler 将保持“永远免费”，以避免社区因将以前免费的工具商业化而感到愤怒。 在 Telerik 之前，我曾与一位潜在收购者交谈过，他估计将另一种以前免费的工具商业化的品牌损害是其收购价格的 25 倍，这意味着他们可能永远不会从中获利。

Telerik 宣布这一变化的博客文章非常明确：

… 但即便如此还不够，所以不久之后又发布了后续帖子：

这一明确的承诺意味着改善“Fiddler 业务”意味着我们需要：1) 将 Fiddler 背后的技术货币化（我们有几个可靠的想法），或 2) 转向他们可以销售的新跨平台产品，或 3) 违背承诺并开始对 Windows 版 Fiddler 收费，或 4) 使用 Fiddler 展示（并促进销售）Telerik 的 .NET 组件产品。

当我在 Telerik 时，我在#1 上做了一些工作——我们创建了 FiddlerCore 的可授权版本，FiddlerCore 是 Fiddler 内部的核心引擎，我们的想法是其他公司可以基于它销售产品。 Telerik 在他们的 Test Studio 产品中使用了 FiddlerCore（这就是我开始引起他们注意的原因），我们假设其他公司可能需要类似的技术。 兴趣是…… 不是很高… 部分原因是我们很少努力去传播福音，部分原因是许可证价格将其限制为大公司。

非常令人沮丧和羞辱的是，我的前雇主想在他们的消息分析器产品中使用 FiddlerCore。 但他们不想为此付出代价。 因此，价值数千亿美元的软件巨头编写了代码来提示最终用户盗版 FiddlerCore：

这种行为最常见于试图避免支付 MP3 专利费的可疑应用程序。 直到今天，我仍然对两家公司的律师允许这种体验的传播感到震惊。 （事实上​​，Telerik 的所有客户几乎都是微软生态系统的开发人员，这可能与 Telerik 没有提起诉讼有关）。

在我加入 Telerik 几天后，我开始制定策略#2（构建跨平台版本）。 我花了几个月的时间尝试让 Fiddler 在 Mono 上运行，Mono 是 .NET Framework 的早期跨平台版本，可以在 Mac 和 Linux 上运行。 进展不太顺利。 我为 Linux 构建了一个可用的版本，但 MacOS 的 UI 端口会不断崩溃。 混合策略，使用 Mono for FiddlerCore，并在 Electron 上构建新的前端，似乎是一条可行的前进道路。 遗憾的是，这一愿景在 2014 年被搁置，因为 Telerik 在美国股市预期的 IPO 之前进行了大规模的美国裁员。 在 IPO 失败并随后被 Progress Software 收购后，Telerik 最终重新启动了这一战略，最终推出了 Fiddler Everywhere。 与仅限 Windows 的 Fiddler Classic 相比，Fiddler Everywhere 提供了几个关键优势（跨平台！ 一些团队功能！） 但它也有很多缺点（功能较少，没有可扩展性模型）。

我希望 Progress/Telerik 能够在某个时候开源 Fiddler Classic，以发展生态系统 - 像 Fiddler SAZ 格式这样的东西会变得更加流行，并创造可货币化协同效应的可能性。 唉，这从未发生过。 相反，Fiddler Classic 只是悄然衰落。 随着浏览器采用新标准（例如 http2、h3、GREASE、tls1.3、zstd 内容压缩），Fiddler Classic 需要越来越多的警告和解决方法才能继续使用。 然而，Fiddler 丰富的可扩展性模型意味着，自从我失去了直接向 Fiddler 源代码提交更新的能力后的十年里，我可以继续在 Fiddler 中构建新功能。

我仍然几乎每天在 Windows 上使用 Fiddler，但在很多情况下，我什至不再使用 Fiddler 来捕获流量，而只是将其用作 Chromium 本地捕获的流量的查看器，或者使用它的 TextEncoder 和 Inspectors，甚至用作其他工具的前端。

Progress 添加了一个预下载调查来收集用户电子邮件（烦人！） 并定期直接在 Fiddler Classic UI 内添加调查和广告。 但即使这些有时会产生令人恼火的误导，它们也并不太烦人。

其他价值可疑的变化也只是有点烦人。

本周的地毯拉动

周一打开 Fiddler，我看到了 Fiddler 更新公告，其中包括一些巧妙的改进，特别是对 ZSTD 解压缩的支持（废弃了我的解决方法）：

然而，我并没有立即接受更新，因为我怀疑有什么事情正在发生。 （我也因为 Windows 抱怨安装程序的签名而分心）。

果然，安装程序的第一个屏幕提到了 Fiddler 中的另一个重要更改，该更改在该闪亮的更新公告中并未提及：

Progress Telerik 决定开始要求 Fiddler Classic 不得用于“商业”目的。 除了许可证中的新文本之外，Fiddler 还显示了这个大的橙色条：

所以… Fiddler 的所有者似乎违背了对社区的承诺，该产品不再免费。

与进步对话/Telerik

从字面上看，许可协议规定您不能将 Fiddler Classic 用于商业目的，即使您付费！ 这是相当令人震惊的，因为这意味着 Fiddler 最活跃的用户（他们围绕 Fiddler 构建了扩展和工作流程）无法使用它们，即使他们愿意付费。 这样的立场似乎非常愚蠢，我认为这一定只是一个疏忽。 经我询问，Progress Telerik 提供了以下声明：

不，Progress 不打算通过付费许可提供 Fiddler Classic。 我们认识到 Fiddler Classic 多年来在支持开发人员调试工作流程方面发挥的重要作用。 继续按照商业和企业客户所需的水平投资产品，包括持续的功能开发和平台现代化，不符合我们的长期产品战略。 因此，近年来，Progress 专注于维护和支持 Fiddler Classic，同时将其开发工作转向 Fiddler Everywhere。 也就是说，我们认识到 Fiddler Classic 中提供的可扩展功能的价值。 因此，我们将继续致力于 Fiddler Everywhere 中的脚本功能，以帮助用户以最小的干扰继续他们现有的工作流程。 我们还将继续根据客户需求和用例评估其他功能请求。 一如既往，我们对反馈持开放态度，并致力于了解如何最好地支持我们的用户。

改进的脚本功能可能会满足某些用户的需求，但它绝对不会涵盖当今 Fiddler Classic 所享受的广泛场景，特别是对于构建了自定义检查器、转码器或将 Fiddler 与公司内使用的其他系统和流程集成的其他扩展的用户而言。

在他们回复的最后一段中，Progress/Telerik 产品经理（或者更有可能是他们的律师）似乎试图建议我不应该与你们这些好人分享我的想法（强调我的想法）：

最后但并非最不重要的一点是，Progress 之外的任何人均无权代表公司发布公告、提供评论或回复客户有关 Progress 业务的询问。 所有问题应直接发送至 Progress 的官方沟通渠道 fiddler@progress.com。

不用说，我不代表我的前雇主发言，但他们也不会阻止我谈论这一变化。

我的感受

有些人问我对此有何感想。 简而言之，失望，有些背叛，但最终并不感到惊讶。 Fiddler for Windows 是一款功能强大的工具，可为用户提供巨大的价值，而短期利润最大化的本质是，拥有宝贵资产的公司往往很难认识到不滥用用户的长期价值。

正如我之前在文章中谈到我在构建 Fiddler 时所犯的错误一样，缺乏盈利计划是该产品策略的一个关键缺陷。 当 Telerik 收购 Fiddler 时，我认为那里的商业人士会制定一种超越每周数以万计的下载者“眼球货币化”的策略（尽管仅就流量获取而言，这很划算）。

正如我上面所描述的，可货币化产品策略的开发从未得到任何真正的关注。 与此同时，Postman 的团队假设基于团队的产品将成为赢家，他们相应地定制了他们的产品，在获得 4.33 亿美元的风险投资后，他们的估值飙升至 $5.6B。 我怀疑 Postman 首次公开募股前的真实估值可能更低，但从长远来看，Progress Software 的整个市值目前仅为 $1.7B。

我很高兴最近看到 Progress 通过引入对 MCP 和流行代理的支持，将 Fiddler Everywhere 推向了最热门的技术趋势（人工智能）。 如果做得好，这可能会成为人们愿意花大钱购买的杀手级功能，因为它可以提供价值。

然而，我担心 Progress 可能刚刚蒸发了信任和善意，而这些信任和善意本来可以顺利地将用户从可靠的（如果过时的）免费产品转移到积极开发的具有脱节功能集的付费产品。 尤其如此，因为 Fiddler 的会话存档 Zip (SAZ) 格式可以允许两者之间的兼容性。

我们该何去何从？

许多 Fiddler Classic 用户可以愉快地继续免费使用该产品来满足个人非商业需求。 一些 Fiddler Classic 客户可能会很乐意切换到 Fiddler Everywhere，该产品的功能有限版本的起价为 84 美元/用户/年，或者完整的 Fiddler Everywhere 功能集为 444 美元/用户/年（如上所述，它不具有 Fiddler Classic 的所有功能或与其扩展的兼容性）。

一些用户告诉我，他们已经采取措施禁用 Fiddler 5.x 的升级逻辑，并在其原始许可证下永远保留最终的免费版本。 他们将使用可扩展性模型来使其与现代网络兼容。 不幸的是，旧版安装程序的许可证不允许公开重新分发。

有些用户可能会完全停止使用 Fiddler。 随着浏览器开发人员工具的发展，许多 Web 开发人员的需求现在可以通过各自浏览器中的“网络”选项卡得到充分满足。

一些用户可能会转向竞争产品，无论是付费（Postman、Charles）还是免费开源（mitmproxy）。

提琴手 -> CLeARINET？

Progress 的决定特别令人困惑的一件事是时机。 《Cripping Fiddler》在 2020 年左右可能会产生一些（邪恶的）意义，但如果你没有注意到，时代已经变了。

  • 人工智能代理已经能够快速、廉价地对生产质量的代码进行振动编码。 当 Telerik 之前的收购方问我他们需要多长时间来实施自己的方案时，我猜测大约需要 2000 小时，如果我指导他们的话，大约需要 700 小时。 使用人工智能编码代理，我怀疑你可以在大约 160 小时内完成 90% 的工作。
  • 构建 Fiddler 的大部分工作都是“解决问题”，而用于实现这一目标的资源比以往任何时候都好得多：我们拥有比以往更好的博客、更好的工具、更好的 RFC 和更多的开源代码。
  • .NET 平台比 Fiddler 主要针对的 v2.0 框架的功能要强大得多（特别是与异步相关）。 我已经列出了一系列需要避免的错误和陷阱。
  • 有一个庞大的 .NET 开发人员社区可能有兴趣伸出援手，其中包括最近自愿从 Microsoft 退休的数百人。 还有一些非常聪明的开发人员（Kevin、Jérôme、Chrisx3 等）为旧版 Fiddler 构建了扩展和其他代码，他们可能会抓住机会将他们的 PR 纳入开源替代品。
  • Fiddler 没有“护城河”——SAZ 文件格式简单且易于读写。 该产品旨在与基于开放标准的协议和格式进行交互。 Fiddler 的真正价值几乎完全是“善意”。

改变的时机似乎已经成熟。

当我命名 Fiddler 时，我这样做是因为我是 Microsoft Office 剪贴画团队的一员，而且我知道我们手边有大量免费的小提琴图片。 时间已经过去了，我们已经有了可以生成我们想要的任何图像的人工智能。 我生命中一个重要的孩子演奏单簧管。 如果你眯着眼睛看，Clarinet 听起来有点像“Clear INET”，而清晰地看到互联网流量就是这里的重点。

大约 5 分钟后，我们就得到了名称、域名和启动屏幕。

现在我们只需要一些代码。 :)

我目前正处于工作和生活特别忙碌的时期（这个月我要搬家），但我希望很快在这个领域能取得一些进展和更新。 除非 Progress Software 想要帮我省去麻烦，并为开源 FiddlerClassic 本身赢得大量赞誉！ ;-)

-Eric

本节来自 Fiddler Book。

首先，需要承认的是，Fiddler Web 调试器并不是开发世界上最受欢迎的调试代理的宏伟愿景或雄心的结果。 作为一种必要的工具，我从来没有打算构建一个如此灵活、强大和复杂的平台，以至于我不得不花一年的时间写一本书来解释如何充分利用它。 但我们到了。

在深入讨论技术章节之前，我将首先分享 Fiddler 背后的故事。

1999 年春天，作为马里兰大学的一名学生，我有机会面试 Microsoft 一个新团队的项目管理实习机会。 我的最后一个面试官的第一个问题是“HTTP 是如何工作的？” 由于只了解基础知识，我给出了一个不完整且有些不准确的答案，但并没有让自己太难堪。 那年夏天和接下来的夏天，我致力于研究 SharePoint 第一个版本的功能。 在极少数情况下，我发现自己在 Microsoft Network Monitor (NetMon) 中查看 Web 流量，这是一个功能强大但原始且难以使用的数据包嗅探器。 2001 年初夏，我全职加入 Microsoft，担任 Office Clip Art 客户端和网站的项目经理。

当时，我团队中的大多数开发人员和测试人员都是 Web 开发新手，之前负责用 C 和 C++ 编写本机代码应用程序。 很快我们就发现调试过程过于繁琐——我的许多同事都不愿意使用 NetMon。 我什至看到一些开发人员通过将鼠标悬停在 Visual Studio 中的变量上来调试 HTTP 请求，检查十六进制的原始流量：

在开发了几个小型 Windows 实用程序之后，我确信我可以编写一些代码来使 Web 调试变得更简单。 我的第一个简单的工作是基于现有的 C++ 代理服务器并对其进行少量修改，以便它将 HTTP 流量发送到系统控制台：

可以慷慨地称这种工作为原始——代理无法处理安全流量或身份验证协议。 非文本内容是另一个问题 - 有趣的是，该实用程序会尝试将二进制内容呈现为 ASCII。 老派控制台用户可能还记得八位字节 0x07 代表“响铃”字符，当它显示在控制台中时，会发出系统蜂鸣声。 发布后不久，Office Online 团队的走廊听起来就像拉斯维加斯赌场，因为二进制内容流经每个测试人员办公室中运行的调试代理。

尽管有非常烦人的限制，这个工具仍然很受欢迎，我受到启发开始开发下一个版本。 我用 Borland Delphi 模拟了一个快速的小演示，这是一种用于我当时大部分开发工作的本机代码语言。 丰富多彩的 UI 预示了 Fiddler 最终的出现：

然而，当我思考用本机代码编写代理服务器的安全性和内存管理影响时，我很快决定我的下一步工作将使用 C# 进行开发，这是我最好的朋友刚刚加入的 Visual Studio 团队正在开发的一种新语言。 在 .NET 中从头开始编写 HTTP 代理服务器的想法带来了两个重大挑战：我并不真正了解 HTTP 是如何工作的，而且我不知道如何用 C# 进行编码。

幸运的是，只要去书店几次，周末有很多空闲时间，这两个缺点都会得到弥补。 两本书是我忠实的伴侣：《HTTP：权威指南》和《C# Cookbook》。 我一章又一章地了解了 HTTP 和 C#，一周又一周地了解了 Fiddler。 开始大约六个月后，我准备好了 Fiddler 的基本版本：

与它的前身一样，它也有很多限制（以及数千个错误），但它被同事们热切地采用了，因为我的第一个代理实用程序的不断发出的嘟嘟声使他们的 PC 扬声器面临烧坏的危险。

在随后的几年中，Fiddler 逐渐增强了两个可扩展性模型，一种自动生成和修改响应的机制，以及对安全 (HTTPS) 流量、FTP 和 HTML5 WebSockets 的支持。 2012年，Fiddler被移植到Mono框架，使其能够直接在Mac和Linux PC以及虚拟机上运行。
